A mixed-effects model writes each individual parameter (subject, cell, cell line) as a
population value plus a random deviation, estimates population values and spread, and integrates
the deviations out of the likelihood. In dMod2 random effects are declared in the `parfn`; `em()`
fits by the EM algorithm with one of four approximations of the integral. Example:
theophylline, twelve subjects, one oral dose each, plasma concentrations over a day.

```{r setup}
```

## Pharmacokinetic model

The dose enters a depot, is absorbed into the central compartment of volume $V$ and cleared by the
flux $\mathrm{Cl}\, C_c$ in the unit frame: clearance $\mathrm{Cl}$ is a volume per time, the
concentration falls at rate $\mathrm{Cl}/V$.

```{r reactions}
```

`em()` needs second derivatives: build with `deriv2 = TRUE` and the forward-over-reverse
derivative modes.

```{r model}
```

## Theophylline data

Each subject is a condition; the condition table holds dose in mg and body weight.

```{r data}
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
head(table)
plotData(data) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "time [h]", y = "concentration [mg/L]", color = "Subject")
```

## Random-effect formulas

`define("x <- x", x = ...)` starts the transformation as in [Setting up models](guide-model.html),
`branch()` copies it per table row, and `insert()` sets the dose into the depot, an empty central
compartment and log-scale parameters. An effect formula turns a symbol into a linear predictor with
fixed and random effects in lme4 notation:

```{r trafo}
```

The formula acts after the log transformation, so $\log \mathrm{Cl}_i = \mathrm{Cl} +
\eta_{\mathrm{Cl},i}$, $\eta_{\mathrm{Cl},i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \omega_{\mathrm{Cl}}^2)$: log-normal
individual parameters. Further forms:

- `Cl ~ 1 + (1 | ID)`: random intercept per subject.
- `Cl ~ 1 + logWeight + (1 | ID)`: a covariate, fixed effect `Cl_logWeight` on a table column.
- `Ka + Cl ~ 1 + (1 | p | ID)`: random effects of `Ka` and `Cl` correlated (same ID `p`).
- `Cl ~ 1 + wt + (1 + dose | p | ID)`: a covariate and a random slope, correlated with the
  intercept.
- `Cl ~ 1 + (1 | ID) + (1 | ID:OCC)`: variability between subjects and between occasions.
- `Cl ~ 1 + (1 | gr(ID, dist = spikeSlab()))`: spike-and-slab instead of normal random effects.

A group (a level of the grouping, such as a subject) may own several conditions, which share the
group random effects; a condition outside every group has none. The random effects of one ID, or of one
term without ID, form a block with full covariance, so $\Omega$ is block diagonal; `omega_<a>_<b>`
are the entries of the Cholesky factor of each block, with the log of the factor diagonal on the diagonal,
for a random effect alone in a block the log of the standard deviation of that effect.
This chapter treats normal random effects; spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process ones are in
[Sparse deviations](guide-sparse-deviations.html).

## Marginal likelihood

`em()` maximizes the likelihood of fixed effects, $\Omega$ and error parameters with the random
effects of every group integrated out. It takes the data objective
`normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e)` and builds the random-effect prior from `randomEffects(p)`;
`normT(..., df = 4)` instead of `normL2()` gives Student-t residuals. `method` picks the
approximation:

| method | use | reported $-2 \log L$ |
|---|---|---|
| `"focei"` | default, fast, Laplace's approximation at the modes | Laplace |
| `"quadrature"` | skewed posteriors, few random effects per group | quadrature |
| `"laplaceEM"` | EM on the Laplace approximation | quadrature of level $K + 2$ |
| `"saem"` | many random effects per group, non-Gaussian posteriors | quadrature of level $K + 2$ |

$K$ is the number of random effects of a group. Derivations: [Methods > Marginal likelihood](methods-nlme.html#marginal-likelihood) and
[Methods > EM algorithm](methods-nlme.html#em-algorithm).

## First-order conditional estimation (FOCEI)

First-order conditional estimation with interaction replaces each integral by Laplace's
approximation at the mode of the group; $-2 \log L$ may lie above or below the exact one. Inner
and outer trust regions and gradient: [Methods > FOCEI](methods-nlme.html#focei).

### FOCEI fit

`init` holds the parameters that are neither random effects nor created by effect formulas (those
start at 0); random-effect standard deviations start at `control$sd`.

```{r focei, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
chapter <- stored("results/guide-nlme.rds", "results/guide-nlme.R", envir = new.env())
obj <- normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e)
# the model of the fit, which the saved result leaves out, from an evaluation at the estimates
model <- c("prdfn", "data", "errfn", "design")
fit <- chapter$fit
fit[model] <- em(obj, random, fit, control = list(trustControl = list(iterlim = 0), boundary = FALSE),
                 verbose = FALSE)[model]
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
summary(fit)
```

Every block here holds one random effect, so `omega_*` are log standard deviations, shown on
natural scale in the random-effects table.
Shrinkage near 0 means the modes spread as widely as the random effects, near 1 that the data of a
subject hardly move the individual parameter.

`value` is $-2 \log L$ with all data constants; `valueNonmem`, $-2 \log L$ less $\log(2\pi)$ per
reading above the limit of quantification, compares with the NONMEM `OBJ` (`NA` for `normT()`). The fit holds `argument`, `Omega`,
`omega` (standard deviations and correlations with standard errors), `random` (modes per group with
conditional standard errors), `etaModes`, `etaSE` and `shrinkage`. Methods: `coef()`, `vcov()`,
`confint()` (Wald or `method = "profile"`), `logLik()`, `AIC()`, `BIC()`, `anova()` of nested fits,
`predict()` (individual and population), `residuals()`, `simulate()` and the plots below.

### FOCEI settings

| entry of `control` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `sd` | `0.3` | start of standard deviations not in `init` |
| `innerControl` | `rinit = 1`, `rmax = 10`, `iterlim = 30`, `steptol = 1e-8`, `mtol = 1e-12` | trust region of the modes |
| `trustControl` | `rinit = 1`, `rmax = 10`, `iterlim = 200`, `ftol = 1e-7`, `mtol = 1e-5` | trust region of population parameters |
| `derivMode` | `"forward-reverse"` | volume-term second derivatives, or `"forward-forward"` |
| `secondOrderCorrection` | `TRUE` | derivative of the volume term |

`"forward-forward"` needs `deriv2 = TRUE`; `summary()` says whether the Hessian is exact;
`secondOrderCorrection = FALSE` biases the estimates
([Methods > Volume term](methods-nlme.html#volume-term)). `fixed` holds parameters at given values.
`sparse = TRUE` uses sparse Hessians for many fixed effects, `"auto"` decides as `trust()`. The
outer `mtol` is a predicted change of $10^{-5}$ in $-2 \log L$, the inner tolerances are tighter;
the solver error must stay below them. `em(cores = )` spreads groups and conditions over threads,
[Remote computing](guide-remote-computing.html#threads-and-processes).

## Adaptive sparse-grid quadrature

Laplace's approximation biases $\Omega$ most for skewed posteriors, e.g. oral doses sampled near
absorption. `method = "quadrature"` starts from the converged FOCEI fit and integrates on a sparse
grid around each group mode at the level `tol` requires; level $K$ is Laplace's approximation. A
certificate flags groups whose posterior the grid does not resolve. Grid, stages and certificate: [Methods > Adaptive sparse-grid
quadrature](methods-nlme.html#adaptive-sparse-grid-quadrature).

| entry of `control$quadrature` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `tol` | `0.1` | allowed change of $-2 \log L$ by the next level, split over groups; `Inf` keeps stage levels |
| `levels` | `K + 1` | stages; level `K + s` is exact for total degree `2 s + 1` |
| `maxLevel` | `K + 8` | highest level |
| `tolDecrement` | `1e-4` | Newton decrement that ends a stage |
| `maxEcmPerStage` | `10` | rebuilds per stage |
| `cm1Control`, `maxCm1Iter` | `rinit = 1`, `ftol = mtol = 1e-8`; `30` | `trust()` settings and iterations of a step |
| `pruneTol` | `Inf` | drop nodes with log weight this far below the largest |
| `certificate` | `points = 256`, `seed = 1` | importance-sampling check, `FALSE` skips |

A quadrature fit holds `stageTrace` (per rebuild: stage level, value, Newton decrement,
resolution, highest level, node count), `etaCov` (posterior covariance
$\hat M_i - \hat m_i \hat m_i^\top$ per group) and `certificate`. `plotTrace(fit)` draws the trace,
`plotRandomEffects(fit)` histograms and QQ plots of conditional draws, or with `type = "modes"` of
the modes, against the fitted $\mathcal{N}(0, \Omega_{kk})$ (see [Model diagnostics](#model-diagnostics)).

## Laplace EM

`method = "laplaceEM"` runs expectation conditional maximization on the Laplace approximation and
reports the quadrature of level $K + 2$. Settings in `control$quadrature`: convergence tolerance
`epsEcm` (default `1e-5`), iterations `maxEcm` (default 200), and of the quadrature above
`cm1Control`, `maxCm1Iter`, `pruneTol` and `maxLevel`; the levels are $K + 1$ and $K + 2$, and the
fit has no certificate. Details: [Methods > Laplace EM](methods-nlme.html#laplace-em).

## Stochastic approximation EM (SAEM)

`method = "saem"` draws the random effects from the posterior and averages over iterations, after
a burn-in with falling step sizes; suited to many random effects and skewed, heavy-tailed or
multimodal posteriors. `set.seed()` reproduces a fit. `em()` reports the quadrature of level
$K + 2$ at the estimate, with standard errors from the Hessian of that quadrature. Details: [Methods > SAEM](methods-nlme.html#saem).

| entry of `control$saem` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `nBurnin`, `nEM` | `200`, `300` | most burn-in and averaging iterations |
| `nMcmc`, `nLaplace` | `3`, `3` | random-walk and independence steps per iteration |
| `laplaceEvery` | `5` | iterations between mode refreshes |
| `laplaceScale` | `1.5` | covariance factor of the independence proposal |
| `window` | `25` | iterations of drift test and averaging start |
| `mcTol` | `0.05` | Monte Carlo increase of $-2 \log L$ that ends averaging |

## Comparison of methods

The four methods from the same start:

```{r compare, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
fits <- list(focei = fit, quadrature = chapter$quadrature, saem = chapter$saem)
round(sapply(fits, function(f) c(f$argument[names(fit$argument)], minus2logL = f$value)), 3)
```

```{r laplaceem, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
laplaceEM <- chapter$laplaceEM
round(c(laplaceEM$argument[names(fit$argument)], minus2logL = laplaceEM$value), 3)
```

Estimates agree within their standard errors. Each $-2 \log L$ approximates the same integral;
Laplace EM and SAEM report the quadrature. FOCEI may lie below it: Laplace's method is no bound,
and a lower value is approximation error, not a better fit. Stage trace and certificate of the
quadrature fit:

```{r}
fits$quadrature$stageTrace[, c("level", "ecmIter", "OFV", "decrement", "resolution", "maxLevel", "nodes")]
fits$quadrature$certificate
```

`r q <- fits$quadrature$stageTrace; if (nrow(q) == 1 && q$decrement[1] < q$resolution[1]) "Here one rebuild ends the fit: the Newton decrement on the rebuilt nodes lies below what the nodes resolve, so the estimate of FOCEI stands, with the value of the quadrature." else sprintf("Here the fit takes %d rebuilds.", nrow(q))` `r flagged <- sum(fits$quadrature$certificate$flag); if (flagged == 0) "No group is flagged." else sprintf("%d of %d groups are flagged.", flagged, nrow(fits$quadrature$certificate))` `plotTrace()` draws the trace of a fit with
several rebuilds.

## Model diagnostics

`plotCombined()` draws each subject with individual (IPRED, random effects at the modes) and
population prediction (PRED, random effects 0):

```{r, fig.height = 6.5}
plotCombined(fit, ncol = 4) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "time [h]", y = "concentration [mg/L]")
```

Conditional weighted residuals (CWRES) linearize around the modes; normalized prediction
distribution errors (NPDE) come from simulations, decorrelated per subject, without
linearization. Both should look like standard normal noise against prediction and time.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plotResiduals(fit, type = c("CWRES", "NPDE"), nsim = 200, seed = 1)
```

The visual predictive check compares data percentiles with simulated prediction intervals per
time bin.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plotVPC(fit, nsim = 200, bins = 8, seed = 1)
```

Histograms and QQ plots of draws from the conditional distributions of the random effects
against the fitted $\mathcal{N}(0, \Omega_{kk})$:

```{r, fig.height = 5}
plotRandomEffects(fit)
```

Against a covariate, random effects show whether it explains part of the variability:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plotRandomEffects(fit, covariates = table["weight"])
```

## Covariate effects

Clearance and volume usually scale with body weight, entered as a fixed effect on a table column,
centered on log scale:

```{r covariates, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
fit2 <- chapter$fit2
comparison <- anova(fit, fit2)
comparison
```

`anova()` compares nested fits by likelihood ratio. Weight lowers $-2 \log L$ by
`r round(comparison$chisq[2], 2)`, p-value `r round(comparison$p[2], 2)`: among twelve subjects of
similar weight it explains little clearance spread, and the simpler model stays.

## Nested and crossed groups

Further groupings, nested (occasions within subjects) or crossed (patients and centers), are
further formula terms. `em()` integrates them by FOCEI per connected component of the conditions;
the [pharmacometrics project](pharmacometrics.html) fits mavoglurant with between-occasion
variability this way:

```r
insert(trafo, Cl ~ 1 + (1 | ID) + (1 | ID:OCC))
```

Which groups differ at all, rather than by how much: [Sparse deviations](guide-sparse-deviations.html).


## Multistart optimization

`msem()` runs `em()` from `fits` starts, the first at `init`, the others perturbed around it with
standard deviation `sd`, and returns the best fit, all starts in `$multistart`. `theophyllineMultistart.R` of the project
`pharmacometrics` runs 200 starts each for FOCEI, quadrature and SAEM from the same draws:

```{r, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
project <- normalizePath("../../examples/pharmacometrics")
knitr::read_chunk("../../examples/pharmacometrics/theophyllineMultistart.R")
```

```{r multistart, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
saved <- stored(file.path(project, "results", "multistart.rds"),
                file.path(project, "theophyllineMultistart.R"), envir = new.env())
values <- unlist(lapply(saved$multistart, `[[`, "value"))
wide <- diff(range(values, na.rm = TRUE)) > 50
lowest <- vapply(saved$multistart, function(t) sum(t$value < min(t$value, na.rm = TRUE) + 1, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
```

FOCEI waterfall of all 200 starts:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plotValues(saved$multistart$FOCEI, pseudoLog = wide)
```

Quadrature and SAEM, both valued by the quadrature, so comparable:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plotValues(saved$multistart[c("quadrature", "SAEM")], pseudoLog = wide)
```

All three methods find the same two optima, with method-specific $-2 \log L$. Most starts end on
the upper plateau, the fit above; about `r round(mean(lowest))` of
`r nrow(saved$multistart[[1]])` per method reach the lower one, the flip-flop solution:

```{r}
flipflop <- saved$best$FOCEI
signif(rbind(fit = c(exp(fit$argument[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")]), minus2logL = fit$value),
             flipflop = c(exp(flipflop[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")]),
                          minus2logL = min(saved$multistart$FOCEI$value, na.rm = TRUE))), 4)
```

With one oral dose and no intravenous data, absorption and elimination can swap. In the flip-flop
solution absorption is the slow step, the volume shrinks to
`r round(exp(flipflop[["V"]]), 1)` L and the `Ka` random effect vanishes. The likelihood prefers it
by `r round(fit$value - min(saved$multistart$FOCEI$value, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`, but theophylline
spreads through the body water, about 0.5 L/kg, not a few liters; drug knowledge or a prior on `V`
selects the upper plateau.

### Zero variance components

At the flip-flop solution the `Ka` variance runs to 0. `em()` returns the fit with that variance at
0 and names it in `fit$boundary`; `control$boundary` (default 0.1) is the accepted rise of
$-2 \log L$, `FALSE` switches it off
([Methods > Zero variance components](methods-nlme.html#variance-at-the-boundary)). On the lower
plateau every method does so:

```{r}
sapply(saved$multistart, function(t) sum(t$boundary == "omega_Ka_Ka"))
sapply(saved$best, function(b) signif(b[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")], 4))
```

`theophyllineMultistart.R` refits the best fit of each method by every other method from the
estimates of that fit:

```{r crosscheck, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
saved$cross
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
byMethod <- split(saved$cross$value, saved$cross$by)
quadratureValue <- mean(byMethod$quadrature)
# a bound on the distance of SAEM to the quadrature, one significant digit
saemGap <- max(abs(byMethod$SAEM - quadratureValue))
saemGap <- ceiling(saemGap / 10^floor(log10(saemGap))) * 10^floor(log10(saemGap))
```

From every start each method reaches the same estimates, with method-specific $-2 \log L$: FOCEI
about `r signif(quadratureValue - mean(byMethod$FOCEI), 2)` below the quadrature, which integrates
more accurately than Laplace's method; SAEM, valued by the quadrature of level $K + 2$ at the SAEM
estimate, within `r saemGap` of it.

`msem()` draws all starts and seeds before spreading fits over `cores`, so `set.seed()` reproduces
a run; `cores = c(fits = , conditions = )` splits cores between parallel fits and threads, see
[Remote computing](guide-remote-computing.html#threads-and-processes). Every start runs to
convergence; `plotValues()` draws `$multistart` as a waterfall.

Reference: `randomEffects()`, `em()`, `msem()`, `anova()`, `plotResiduals()`, `plotVPC()`,
`plotRandomEffects()`, `plotTrace()`, `plotValues()`
